clue.text: Such a frosty atmosphere responsible for beastly idol's lack of balls?

definitions.text: Such a frosty atmosphere responsible for beastly idol's lack of balls?

parts.words: Such a frosty atmosphere responsible for beastly idol's lack of balls

explanation.surface: Someone blames an icy spell for a statue of an animal that has lost its testicles.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase comes from the British saying 'cold enough to freeze the balls off a brass monkey'; the beastly idol is the brass monkey itself.
explanation.definitionFit: This informal British idiom names extremely cold conditions, the kind of bitter chill the saying describes.

clue.text: This country smart-arse is without sex

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the brainy word goes round

parts.note: a brain is a clever person, here a mocking know-all
it is a coy word for sex

explanation.surface: Somebody complains that a clever-clogs in this country gets no sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' seems to mean lacking, but here it means outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Private Eye is a British magazine, so this country is the setter's own homeland.

clue.text: Radio Times nit-picker's after the head of Anna Sewell, Brian

indicators.note: the abbreviation and the nit-picker come after Anna's first letter in the answer
the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the name supplies its first letter
RT is the abbreviation of the British TV listings magazine
a critic finds fault, with 's read as is

explanation.surface: A fussy reviewer in a TV magazine follows Anna Sewell, author of Black Beauty, and Brian.
explanation.walkthrough: Brian Sewell was a famously waspish British art critic for the London Evening Standard; the comma turns the name into a reverse-order listing.
explanation.definitionFit: Brian Sewell was famous for writing reviews of exhibitions, an example of this profession.

clue.text: Queen Elizabeth's first involvement in wild bash

indicators.note: the letter is involved in, set inside, the jumbled letters
wild means disordered, so the letters are shaken up

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: first takes just the first letter of the name

parts.note: the name gives its first letter

explanation.surface: The Queen gets involved in a riotous party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queen Elizabeth' reads as one name, but Queen is the definition and only Elizabeth gives a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical Queen of Sheba visited King Solomon, so the name stands for a royal ruler.

clue.text: Duff ITV pollster left right out of stalemate election

indicators.note: duff is British slang for broken or useless, so the letters are mangled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: out, read with of, says left and right are put out of the word pollster; this takes away the second
part of the phrase out of, which removes left and right from the word pollster; this takes away the first

parts.note: taken as written, before its two letters are removed

explanation.surface: A useless TV pollster gets the result of a deadlocked election wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: ITV is a British television network. The definition is loose: a divided vote is what produces a deadlock.
explanation.definitionFit: A vote divided between rival choices tends to produce no clear winner, a deadlock at the ballot box.

clue.text: Spill the beans repeatedly and then stir

indicators.note: repeatedly says the word for spilling the beans is given twice

parts.note: to sing is slang for informing to the police

explanation.surface: An informer keeps talking and then causes trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stir' looks like a verb but it is slang for prison: Sing Sing is the New York state prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Sing Sing is a notorious American jail, and stir is slang for a prison.

clue.text: Donald Dewar, right to replace date, snarled "That's Jack Straw's baby!"

indicators.note: snarled means tangled, so the letters are knotted into a new order
right is put in where the date's letter stood, one letter swapped for another in the name

parts.note: taken as written, before one letter is swapped

explanation.surface: Scottish Labour minister Donald Dewar growls about a colleague's pet project.
explanation.walkthrough: Donald Dewar and Jack Straw were ministers in Blair's government; Straw was Home Secretary, in charge of policing and crime.
explanation.definitionFit: As Home Secretary, Straw's pet policy area was policing and crime, the upholding of the rule of law.

clue.text: Kate's kinky nylons, almost half gone, rustle

indicators.note: kinky means twisted, so the name's letters are bent into a new order

parts.note: the name, with 's read as is

indicators.note: four of the nine letters, just under half, are dropped from the end

parts.note: nylons are women's stockings

explanation.surface: Kate's kinky nylons, half torn off, make a rustling sound.
explanation.walkthrough: Rustle looks like a sound, but it means to steal livestock; a cattle rustler literally takes stock.
explanation.definitionFit: Rustling is stealing farm animals, so taking stock read literally is a joke version of the crime.

clue.text: Love to take speed and get on one's soap-box

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, a nought-shaped letter
rate is speed, as in a rate of knots

explanation.surface: A lover hurries off to deliver a rant.
explanation.definitionFit: To declaim pompously, as a street speaker standing on a box does, is to make a speech.

clue.text: Build on the extremes of Lundy, getting in the way of excited member

definitions.text: in the way of excited member

parts.note: to erect a building is to build it

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: an island in the Bristol Channel, giving its outer letters

explanation.surface: Someone builds on Lundy island and obstructs an overexcited member of the club.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a smutty joke: an aroused member stands upright.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means in an upright manner, the way an aroused penis stands.

clue.text: Party to the secret trendy article on Ken

parts.note: in means fashionable
the is the definite article
to ken is Scots and dialect for to know

explanation.surface: A fashionable Ken is let in on a secret.
explanation.walkthrough: Ken looks like a man's name, but here it is the old verb meaning to know.
explanation.definitionFit: Being informed about something not generally known is an idiom for sharing a confidence.

clue.text: Jack put Kelvin on church body!

parts.note: K is the symbol for the kelvin, the unit of temperature
the nave is the main body of a church

explanation.surface: Someone called Jack has a man named Kelvin put on the church council.
explanation.definitionFit: In a pack of cards the jack is also called the knave, the playing card below the queen.

clue.text: Potential lifesavers, dry pants

parts.note: to air laundry is to dry it
bags is old British slang for loose trousers

explanation.surface: Dry trousers could save your life.
explanation.walkthrough: Pants looks like a verb (gasps), but it is the noun for trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: Inflatable cushions in a car deploy in a crash and can prevent fatal injuries to passengers.

clue.text: Labour's after little number that's easy

indicators.note: the word for labour comes after the short number in the answer

parts.note: no. is the short form of number
labour is sweat, with 's read as is

explanation.surface: A Labour slogan says a minor figure finds things simple.
explanation.walkthrough: Labour looks like the political party; here it simply means hard work.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal phrase is used to say a task is simple and causes no trouble.

clue.text: Being observant, it could therefore be marzipan

definitions.meaning: first meaning: paying attention, spotting things
second meaning, read as two words: something that is ... could be marzipan, the other cake covering

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as NOT ICING: on a cake, the layer under the icing is often marzipan.
explanation.definitionFit: Spotting or perceiving things is the present participle of the verb that means to observe.

clue.text: Palatable way to get rid of a persistent hack

definitions.text: Palatable way to get rid of a persistent hack

parts.words: Palatable way to get rid of a persistent hack

explanation.walkthrough: Hack suggests a dogged reporter, but a hacking cough is the thing to be got rid of.
explanation.definitionFit: A medicated lozenge is a sweet-tasting tablet taken to soothe a sore throat and a tickly cough.

clue.text: See 1
Is no laggard in hanging onto the police's authority?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: does not fall behind, stays level
second meaning: PACE is the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984, which governs British police powers, and this retains it

explanation.walkthrough: PACE is the British Police and Criminal Evidence Act, which sets police powers of arrest and detention.
explanation.definitionFit: To match others' speed is an idiom for not falling behind; the second sense keeps hold of a statute.

clue.text: Country BMW re-styled with baize

indicators.note: something re-styled is given a new form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A luxury car is refitted with green felt upholstery.
explanation.definitionFit: Zimbabwe is a nation in southern Africa, formerly Rhodesia.

clue.text: Boner gets member out of bed

parts.note: cock is slang for the male member
up means risen from bed

explanation.surface: A smutty picture of a man rising in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: Boner looks smutty, but it is old slang for a blunder.
explanation.definitionFit: A boner is a silly mistake, and the British slang word for a botched job means the same.

clue.text: Intimidate then have sex with a western guy

parts.note: to cow is to frighten into submission
poke is crude slang for this

explanation.surface: A bullying seduction of a man from the Wild West.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowpoke is American slang for a cowboy, the stock hero of a Western film.

clue.text: John Thomas, master pillock!

parts.note: John Thomas is a slang name for the penis
a head is a headmaster, the master of a school

explanation.surface: Someone shouts insults at a man named John Thomas who runs a school.
explanation.walkthrough: A pillock is a British insult for a stupid person.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are coarse British insults for a stupid or contemptible person.

clue.text: As the rapper would say, newspapers get a person down

indicators.note: a rapper would say the press as da press, giving the sounds of the answer

parts.note: the press, said in rap slang as da press

explanation.surface: A rapper complains that the newspapers bring people down.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is on a stereotyped rap accent turning 'the' into 'da'.
explanation.definitionFit: To depress someone is to make them feel low or dejected.

clue.text: Label some megastar 'manic'

indicators.note: only some of these words are used, a run of letters inside them

parts.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: Someone sticks the label 'manic' on a celebrity.
explanation.walkthrough: Label looks like a verb, but it is a fashion label.
explanation.definitionFit: Armani is an Italian fashion house, a designer brand name.

clue.text: See 1
Snake in the grass computer!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the common viper, a snake found in grassland
second meaning: one who adds up figures

explanation.walkthrough: Snake in the grass usually means a traitor, but here it is a literal snake.
explanation.definitionFit: The adder is a British viper, and an adder is also anyone or anything that sums numbers.

clue.text: Blair's opener: "Everything's improving" — right fiasco that proves to be

indicators.note: the opener of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the former Prime Minister's name supplies its first letter
everything is all, with 's kept as an S
things that are improving are on the up

explanation.surface: Tony Blair's optimistic first slogan that all is getting better turned out to be a disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls New Labour's 1997 anthem 'Things Can Only Get Better'; 'that proves to be' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This coarse British slang term means a complete mess or bungled job, and a right one is a real disaster.

clue.text: Pissed but looking brilliant?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: in British slang, drunk

explanation.walkthrough: Pissed is British slang for drunk, not American angry.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is slang for drunk and also describes something illuminated, glowing with light.

clue.text: See 5
Judge Baer a right tit, unfortunately

indicators.note: unfortunately means things went wrong, so the letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A judge named Baer is insulted as a right tit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judge' looks like the title of Baer, but it is the definition, used as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To arbitrate is to settle a dispute as a referee would.

clue.text: Oh, puerile, doddery Edward Heath?

indicators.note: doddery means shaky and unsteady, so the letters totter into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A mocking cry at the elderly, childish former Prime Minister Edward Heath.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Heath was the British Prime Minister who took the UK into the European Community in 1973; the question mark marks him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Heath was a famous enthusiast for European integration, an example of a supporter of Europe.

clue.text: Equals a tabloid editor, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly signals that the editor's name is heard, not spelt

parts.note: Piers Morgan edited the News of the World and the Daily Mirror

explanation.surface: A tabloid editor is said to be just as good as anyone.
explanation.walkthrough: The editor is Piers Morgan, a well-known British tabloid editor at the time.
explanation.definitionFit: Peers are people of the same rank or standing, so they are one another's equals.
